newsitem.title: CUBA: BASEBALL-CUBA CANCELS BASEBALL SERIES WITH U.S. AFTER EXPLOSIONS.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-CUBA CANCELS BASEBALL SERIES WITH U.S. AFTER EXPLOSIONS.

text.p: Cuba withdrew at the last minute Monday from a series of baseball games against the United States, citing fears for the safety of players and saying one reason for the cancellation was the weekend bombing of two Havana hotels.
A statement by the Cuban national sports body INDER said it had decided conditions for the eight-game series due to start Tuesday were "not favourable for our team."
It added there would be a "real danger for the personal safety of our players."
Two small bombs exploded within minutes of each other Saturday in the lobbies of the Hotel Nacional and Hotel Capri, slightly injuring three people and causing damage to windows and furniture.

A brief Interior Ministry statement said the ministry had evidence to show that the people responsible for the bombs and the material used were from the United States. The ministry gave no other details.

But official suspicion was likely to fall on hardline groups among the Cuban exile community in Miami opposed to President Fidel Castro's communist government. Some of these groups have carried out violent action in the past, or have threatened to do so.

The director of the U.S. baseball squad, Mike Fiore, said the news of the Cuban cancellation was a "heavy blow." He added the U.S. Baseball Federation stood to lose some $75,000 to $100,000 because of the cancellation.
The baseball series between the United States and Cuba has been held annually for more than a decade. This year's games were to start in Norwich, Connecticut.

The INDER statement said the Saturday bombings added to other issues, including reported plans by hardline Cuban exile groups, which it termed "the Miami counter-revolutionary mafia," to harass the Cuban team during the series.
The statement also cited the "constant provocations" that the national squad has been subjected to in the United States, including pressure on players to defect.
In the last six years, several Cuban star players have defected to the United States, to the dismay of authorities.

They include pitchers Osvaldo Fernandez and Rene Arocha, both with the San Francisco Giants, Livan Hernandez with the Florida Marlins, Rolando Arrojo with Tampa, and shortstop Rey Ordonez with the New York Mets.
The INDER statement did not mention these cases.

But it said that during past visits the Cuban baseball squad had suffered "threatening phone calls, offers of gifts so they defect, and the actual presence in those places (team hotels) of people who knock on the door of players' rooms making the same proposals to them."
The United States and Cuba have no diplomatic relations and have been politically hostile since the 1959 revolution that brought Castro to power.

But despite a 35-year U.S. economic embargo on Cuba, sports exchanges are permitted, and political differences sometimes briefly evaporate in sporting competition, particularly when it involves the two countries' shared passion for baseball.

The talent of some Cuban amateur baseball players, coupled with their low earnings and the island's poor living standards, has led to huge pressure in the past for them to defect to the United States.
